posts.cooked:
I work with supplier price lists and stock files a lot, and I’ve seen some wild ones — codes that don’t match anything, sizes in three different systems, a price hiding in a column called ‘notes’.

What’s the worst file you’ve had to deal with? What broke first when you tried to import it?

Hi @Badhon_Rafi Welcome To Shopify Community So First Of All From client files I’ve handled, the first thing to break is usually the SKUs. Excel quietly drops leading zeros or turns long codes into scientific notation, so the import matches the wrong products or creates duplicates. Next is anything numeric stored as text, like prices with currency symbols or commas as decimals, which import as zero or fail. Sizes in different formats (S/M/L, numeric and EU/US mixed) come after that, because Shopify treats each spelling as a separate variant. The worst files I’ve seen also had merged cells and header rows repeated halfway down. What helped was cleaning a small test batch first and importing just 10 rows before running the full file. please do not forget to like and mark it solution

Hi @Mustafa_Ali, thanks for sharing this — the SKU point rings true for me. Yes, I think that matched / not-matched report by SKU would be genuinely useful. In the supplier files I work with, a bad SKU is usually what creates duplicates or matches the wrong product, and I only find out after the import. Seeing upfront how many rows matched and which ones didn’t — and keeping variant rows grouped with their product instead of splitting them off — would let me fix the file first instead of cleaning up afterwards.

Hi @Badhon_Rafi,

That sounds too familiar! One of the worst files I’ve ever worked with included inventory levels formatted as text rather than numbers, mixed-up variant SKUs, and prices concealed under sporadic text remarks.

Due to the columns’ total misalignment, the system failed on variant mapping as soon as it attempted to import it, generating enormous error logs. Before a successful import was possible, hours of manual spreadsheet work were required to clean up that mess!

Thanks!

Hi @websensepro, that combination is the worst — especially inventory stored as text and prices buried in notes. When the columns shift like that, variant mapping is usually the first thing to break.

What’s helped me most is fixing the file before it ever touches Shopify: match every row by SKU first, keep each variant row tied to its parent product, and run a quick matched / not-matched check. That way the unmatched rows are the only ones I have to look at, instead of digging through a huge error log after a failed import.

Do you usually get a chance to clean the file first, or does it go straight to import?
Before performing any imports, I always want to examine and prepare the spreadsheet locally. Compared to handling error logs following a failed upload, it undoubtedly reduces debugging time.

Badhon_Rafi:

I work with supplier price lists and stock files a lot, and I’ve seen some wild ones — codes that don’t match anything, sizes in three different systems, a price hiding in a column called ‘notes’.

What’s the worst file you’ve had to deal with? What broke first when you tried to import it?

The worst ones for us were PDF order forms built as a size grid: style down the side, sizes across the top, and the quantity sitting in the cell where they meet. They look tidy to a person, but an import sees one row with eight unlabelled numbers. What broke first was sizes. The same supplier used S/M/L on tops, 8/10/12 on dresses and 36/38/40 on the European range, all on one form, and none of it matched the size names already in the Shopify store.

Close second: the supplier code that changes every season for the same product, so the “new” style matches nothing, or worse, matches last year’s style that happens to share the code.

What I learned building the import side of Ezy-OTB (disclosure: I build it): don’t try to make one parser understand every format. Read the file into lines, then let a person confirm the uncertain matches, especially sizes and codes, before anything touches stock. A wrong match that slips through costs far more to fix than the confirm step takes.

posts.cooked: Hi @websensepro, completely agree — cleaning it locally first is the part that saves the most time. What I usually do is run a small test batch first, maybe 10 rows, and fix the SKU, price and stock columns there before the full file goes in. That way the error log stays small enough to actually read, instead of hundreds of lines after a failed import.

Hi @Ernst_1, that size-grid example is a painful one — I’ve seen the same thing with sizes in three different systems on one file. The bit that catches people is that Shopify treats each size spelling as a separate variant, so a mismatch doesn’t just fail, it creates duplicates you have to clean up later. Checking the uncertain size and code matches by hand on a small batch first is slower up front, but it’s still much quicker than fixing wrong stock afterwards.
